name: Force stop and force quit
plain: A person can kill an app: Android force stop cancels alarms; iOS force quit stops background fetch and silent push.
meaning: Marks the clearest signal that someone does not want an app active. Both systems then block background starts until the person opens the app again.

android.persistence: App stays in the stopped state until the user launches it; alarms, jobs and broadcasts cancelled; FCM not delivered
android.note: Stopped state blocks FCM broadcasts and cancels alarms and jobs; Android 15 can also cancel on swipe for some devices

ios.persistence: Background fetch, BG tasks and silent push stop until the user relaunches; location region events still relaunch
ios.api_surface: UIApplication state; no API to detect
ios.note: Apple: force quit means silent push is discarded; VoIP, location and BLE wakes continue for some modes

limits.headline: Can't keep running or wake itself after you force stop (Android) or swipe it away (iPhone)
limits.user_action: You tap Force stop in Android Settings, or swipe the app up in the iPhone app switcher
can: Start working again as soon as you open the app yourself
Wake up for VoIP calls, location events or Bluetooth on iPhone, for some modes only
Keep its saved data, since force stopping does not erase anything
cannot: Receive push messages on Android until you open the app again
Fire alarms or scheduled jobs on Android after a force stop; they are cancelled
Get silent background pushes on iPhone after a force quit; Apple discards them
Run background refresh on iPhone until you open the app once more
limits.differs: Android force stop blocks pushes and cancels alarms. iPhone force quit blocks silent pushes and refresh, but some call, location and Bluetooth wakes still work.

story.what_it_is: A person can kill an app for good, and the phone then blocks it from running in the background.

marketing.name: Close an app
marketing.pitch: Apple documents how to close an app on iPhone by swiping up in the app switcher.

story.for_you: You swipe the app away or tap Force stop. From then on the app cannot send alerts or sync until you open it again, which can surprise you when a reminder never shows up.
story.for_makers: Makers treat a force stop as a clear sign someone wants out. They know push and timed jobs will fail, so they design gentle re-engagement for the next time the user returns.

use_cases.example: After you force quit a chat app, messages stop arriving as alerts until you open it.
A step counter or sleep tracker stops logging in the background and leaves a gap in your day.
A game with timed energy refills cannot send you the full energy alert after you force close it.
An ad measurement tool sees a gap in sessions and cannot record background events until the next open.
A product team sees a spike of users who force stop right after an update and treats it as a quality warning.
A banking app cannot run its background fraud checks after a force stop, so it checks again at next launch.

story.android_note: Force stop sets a stopped state that blocks broadcasts and cancels alarms and jobs.
story.ios_note: Force quit makes iOS discard silent pushes. Some wake ups like VoIP and location can still reach the app.

technical_bounds: Region monitoring and some modes survive force quit on iOS

history.change: Force quit prevents background fetch and silent push
